newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Newspaper urges Asian Australians to oust Hanson.
newsitem.headline: Newspaper urges Asian Australians to oust Hanson.

text.p: An ethnic newspaper is urging Asian Australians to join up and swamp populist politician Pauline Hanson's party and then use their numbers to oust her.
The Chinese Weekly tells its readers in this week's editorial that they owe it to Australia to register themselves as voters.

"Then join with us in becoming members of this repulsive party so we can give it a proper funeral and send Mrs Hanson back to the fish and chip shop where she belongs," Melbourne's Herald-Sun newspaper quoted the Chinese Weekly as saying on Sunday.
The newspaper's owner, Simon Xiang, told the Herald-Sun that 30 initial applications would be sent to Hanson as a test batch.

Hanson, a former fish and chip shop proprietor from conservative Queensland, has attracted about 10 percent voter support with her criticism of multiculturalism, Aborginal welfare, economic reform and immigration, especially Asian immigration.
The major political parties reject her views but she has received enormous publicity in the past year and many of her statements have been endorsed by vocal radio presenters.

The ruling Liberal Party expelled her for racism before her election last year. She nonetheless won a seat in parliament as an independent and earlier this year set up a political party called One Nation.
"This newspaper has legal advice that there is nothing to stop us from joining her One Nation Party and voting in its elections to reject her," the Chinese Weekly said.
Australia's Racial Discrimination Act prevents organisations such as political parties from rejecting members on racial grounds.
Xiang told the Herald-Sun that perhaps 30,000 Asian Australians would respond to the call. One Nation's membership strength is unknown.

The debate that Hanson has stirred up has divided Australia and her political rallies have been accompanied by hostile demonstrations against her, although a gathering in northern Queensland on Saturday passed peacefully.

The Chinese Weekly editorial said: "We have had enough of our children being humiliated at school, our businesses laughed at overseas and feeling unwanted in our chosen home. "It is time to bring this ridicule to an end."
Hanson said in her first speech in parliament last year that Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.

Opponents said the statement was ridiculous. They pointed to statistics showing that less than five percent of the population was born in Asia and noted that she was entirely wrong about the size of Australian's neighbours.
For example, she told parliament that Malaysia's population was 300 million. In fact it is 19 million, about the same as Australia's.
